text: (a) What are isotopes? (b) Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties but different physical properties?
modelAnswer: (a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number (same number of protons) but different mass numbers (different number of neutrons). Example: ¹₁H, ²₁H, ³₁H, or ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C. (b) Chemical properties depend on the number of electrons, especially valence electrons. Isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, so they react the same way. Physical properties such as mass, density, melting and boiling points depend on the mass of the atom. Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses, so their physical properties differ.
keyPoints: Same atomic number, different mass number
Same electronic configuration gives same chemical properties
Different number of neutrons gives different mass and physical properties

text: State one point of difference between: (a) an atom and an ion; (b) the duplet rule and the octet rule.
modelAnswer: (a) An atom is electrically neutral because its number of protons equals its number of electrons. An ion carries a positive or negative charge because it has lost or gained electrons, so its electrons do not equal its protons (e.g. Na has 11 electrons, Na⁺ has 10). (b) Duplet rule: an atom becomes stable with 2 electrons in its only (K) shell, like helium. This applies to H, Li and Be. Octet rule: an atom becomes stable with 8 electrons in its outermost shell, like neon or argon.
keyPoints: Duplet: 2 electrons in outer shell (He configuration)

text: An element has 2 electrons in its fourth shell. State: (i) its electronic configuration; (ii) whether it is a metal or a non-metal; (iii) its valency; (iv) the general name of the elements of the group it belongs to.
modelAnswer: (i) The element fills K, L and M first: 2, 8, 8, 2. This is Calcium, atomic number 20. (In ICSE Class IX the 3d shell is not filled before 4s.) (ii) It is a metal, because it has 2 valence electrons which it loses easily. (iii) Its valency is 2. It loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺. (iv) It belongs to Group 2, the alkaline earth metals.

text: Five atoms are labelled A to E with mass numbers and atomic numbers: A (40, 20), B (19, 9), C (7, 3), D (16, 8), E (14, 7). Which atom: (a) has 20 neutrons in the nucleus; (b) has electronic configuration 2,7; (c) Write the formula of the compound formed between C and D, and state the type of bond.
modelAnswer: (a) A has 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons. (b) B has atomic number 9, so its configuration is 2,7 (Fluorine). (c) C has atomic number 3, so it is Lithium (2,1) with valency 1. D has atomic number 8, so it is Oxygen (2,6) with valency 2. Two Li atoms each give 1 electron to one O atom, so the formula is C₂D, i.e. Li₂O. The bond is ionic (electrovalent).

text: The mass numbers and electronic configurations of five elements are: A (9; 2,2), B (19; 2,7), C (23; 2,8,1), D (28; 2,8,4), E (40; 2,8,8). (a) Name the element which has 22 neutrons. (b) What is the atomic number of C? (c) Write the formula of the compound forming the most stable ionic bond. (d) Write the formula of the compound between B and D.
modelAnswer: Atomic numbers come from the configurations: A = 4 (Be), B = 9 (F), C = 11 (Na), D = 14 (Si), E = 18 (Ar). (a) E has 40 − 18 = 22 neutrons, so the element is Argon. (b) The atomic number of C is 11 (Sodium). (c) The most stable ionic bond forms between the most electropositive metal, C (Na, loses 1 e⁻), and the most electronegative non-metal, B (F, gains 1 e⁻). The compound is CB, i.e. NaF. (d) D (Si) has valency 4 and B (F) has valency 1, so the formula is DB₄, i.e. SiF₄. This is a covalent compound in which Si shares one electron pair with each F.

text: Element X has two valence electrons in its M shell. In element Y, electrons are distributed in the first three shells and Y has eight electrons in its M shell. Element Z has eight electrons in its penultimate shell (M), and its valence shell has fewer electrons than its first shell. (a) Give the electronic configuration of X. (b) Which element among X, Y, Z is inert? (c) In which atom are electrons distributed in all four shells? (d) What is the atomic number of Z? (e) How many electrons and protons are present in Y?
modelAnswer: (a) X has 2 electrons in the M (third) shell as its valence shell, so X = 2,8,2 (Magnesium, Z = 12). (b) Y = 2,8,8 (Argon), which has a complete octet, so Y is inert. (c) Z has M as its penultimate shell, so it has a fourth (N) shell. The first shell holds 2 electrons, so Z's valence shell has fewer than 2, i.e. 1 electron. Z = 2,8,8,1 (Potassium), and Z is the atom with electrons in all four shells. (d) The atomic number of Z is 2 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 19. (e) Y has 18 electrons and 18 protons.

text: Study the table: P (mass number 12, neutrons 6), Q (20, 10), R (23, 12), S (35, 18). (i) Write the atomic number of S. (ii) Write the electronic configuration of R. (iii) To which group does Q belong? (iv) What type of compound (ionic or covalent) is formed by (A) R and S, (B) P and S?
modelAnswer: Atomic number = mass number − neutrons. P = 6 (Carbon), Q = 10 (Neon), R = 11 (Sodium), S = 17 (Chlorine). (i) The atomic number of S is 35 − 18 = 17. (ii) R has atomic number 11, so its configuration is 2,8,1. (iii) Q = 2,8 (Neon) belongs to Group 18 (0), the noble gases. (iv) (A) R (Na, a metal) and S (Cl, a non-metal) form an ionic compound, NaCl, by transfer of an electron. (B) P (C) and S (Cl) are both non-metals, so they form a covalent compound, CCl₄, by sharing electrons.
keyPoints: R + S: ionic (NaCl); P + S: covalent (CCl₄)

text: Differentiate between a group and a period of the periodic table (definition).
modelAnswer: Group: a vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. The modern table has 18 groups. Period: a horizontal row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells, and their properties change gradually across the period. There are 7 periods.
keyPoints: Group: vertical column, same valence electrons, similar properties
Period: horizontal row, same number of shells

text: Study the extract of the periodic table (letters are not the actual symbols). Period 1: A (Group 1), H (Group 18). Period 2: C (Group 13), D (Group 14), E (Group 15), P (Group 16). Period 3: B (Group 1), G (Group 17), F (Group 18). Period 4: Q (Group 18). State which element: (a) forms an electrovalent compound with G; (b) is non-metallic and has a valency of 2; (c) is an inert gas; (d) is the most non-metallic element in the given table; (e) What type of bond is present in a molecule of G?
modelAnswer: Identities: A = H, H = He, C = B (boron), D = C (carbon), E = N, P = O, B = Na, G = Cl, F = Ar, Q = Kr. (a) B (sodium, a Group 1 metal) gives its single valence electron to G (chlorine) and forms the electrovalent compound BG (NaCl). (b) P (oxygen, Group 16, configuration 2,6) is a non-metal with valency 2. (c) H, F or Q (He, Ar, Kr). All are Group 18 inert gases. (d) G (chlorine, Group 17). Halogens are the most non-metallic, readily gaining one electron. (e) G₂ (Cl₂) has a single covalent bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons.
keyPoints: P (O) is a non-metal with valency 2
H, F, Q are inert gases
G₂ has a single covalent bond

text: A periodic arrangement compares elements to the notes of music (sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni). (a) Name the scientist who proposed this periodic table. (b) Did this system work well for the heavier or the lighter elements? (c) What is the significance of the musical notes in this table?
modelAnswer: (a) John Newlands, through his Law of Octaves (1866). (b) It worked well only for the lighter elements, up to calcium. After calcium the pattern broke down, and it had no place for noble gases discovered later. (c) Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of atomic mass. He found that every eighth element had properties similar to the first, just as the eighth note in a musical scale repeats the first (sa … sa). The musical notes show this repetition of properties at every eighth element.
keyPoints: Worked only for lighter elements (up to calcium)
Every eighth element resembles the first, like musical octaves

text: With reference to Mendeleev's periodic table: (a) What was the basis of classification? (b) Which group of elements was not known at that time? (c) Why was the table later replaced (state its main drawbacks)?
modelAnswer: (a) Elements were arranged in increasing order of atomic weight (atomic mass), with elements of similar properties placed in the same group. (b) The noble gases (Group 18 / zero group) had not been discovered. (c) Main drawbacks: (i) Isotopes have different atomic masses but would need different places, yet they are the same element. (ii) In some places the order of atomic mass had to be broken, e.g. Co (58.9) before Ni (58.7) and Ar before K. (iii) Hydrogen had no fixed position. (iv) Chemically dissimilar elements were placed together. After Moseley showed that atomic number is more fundamental, the table was replaced by the Modern (long form) Periodic Table based on atomic number.
keyPoints: Anomalies: isotopes, Co/Ni, Ar/K, position of hydrogen
Replaced by Modern Periodic Table based on atomic number

text: Based on the periodic table: A (atomic no. 11), B (12), C (14), E (16), F (17), G (18) all lie in one period. (i) Give the period number of C. (ii) Give the configuration of the element that would be directly above A. (iii) What is the name of the elements of Group 17 (VIIA) and what does the name mean? (iv) Why is the placement of G in this period logical?
modelAnswer: (i) C has atomic number 14 (2,8,4), with 3 shells, so it is in Period 3. (ii) A is sodium (2,8,1). The element above it in Group 1 is lithium, configuration 2,1. (iii) Group 17 elements are called halogens, which means 'salt producers'. They react with metals to form salts such as NaCl. (iv) G has atomic number 18 (2,8,8), argon. It has 3 shells, so it belongs to Period 3, and its outer shell is a complete octet, so it ends the period as a noble gas in Group 18.
keyPoints: G = Ar (2,8,8): 3 shells, complete octet, ends Period 3

text: Match the atomic numbers 4, 8, 10, 15 and 19 with each of the following: (a) an element which can form a trivalent ion; (b) an element with 4 shells; (c) an element with 6 valence electrons; (d) an element which does not form an ion; (e) an element that belongs to the alkaline earth metals group.
modelAnswer: Configurations: 4 = 2,2 (Be); 8 = 2,6 (O); 10 = 2,8 (Ne); 15 = 2,8,5 (P); 19 = 2,8,8,1 (K). (a) 15 (P): it gains 3 electrons to form P³⁻. (b) 19 (K): 2,8,8,1 has 4 shells. (c) 8 (O): 2,6. (d) 10 (Ne): it has a complete octet, so it is inert. (e) 4 (Be): 2,2, Group 2.

text: (a) Name a stable negative ion which has the same electronic configuration as argon. (b) Write the period and group of the element with atomic number 3. (c) Similar chemical properties are seen for elements in the periodic table at regular intervals. What is the reason for this pattern?
modelAnswer: (a) Chloride ion, Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Also S²⁻ (sulphide) or P³⁻. (b) Atomic number 3 is lithium (2,1): Period 2, Group 1 (IA). (c) Chemical properties depend on the number of valence electrons. When elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, the same outer-shell configuration recurs at regular intervals (after 2, 8, 8, 18 … elements). Elements with the same number of valence electrons therefore show similar properties. This is periodicity.
keyPoints: Cl⁻ (or S²⁻) is isoelectronic with Ar

text: Give reasons: (a) Alkali metals are strong reducing agents. (b) Noble gases do not combine with other elements to form molecules. (c) Halogens are good oxidising agents. (d) Alkali metals and halogens do not occur free in nature.
modelAnswer: (a) Alkali metals have only one valence electron and low ionisation energy, so they lose that electron very easily. A substance that donates electrons is a reducing agent. (b) Noble gases have a stable, completely filled outer shell (an octet, or a duplet for He). They have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, so they have zero valency and do not form molecules. (c) Halogens have 7 valence electrons, high electronegativity and high electron affinity, so they readily gain one electron to complete their octet. A substance that accepts electrons is an oxidising agent. (d) Both are extremely reactive: alkali metals lose an electron easily and halogens gain one easily. They therefore always occur combined in compounds such as NaCl and KCl, not as free elements.
keyPoints: Alkali metals: 1 valence electron, easily lost → reducing
Noble gases: complete octet/duplet → zero valency
High reactivity → occur only in compounds

text: Draw electron dot diagrams for the formation of: (a) Magnesium chloride [Mg = 12, Cl = 17] (b) Water molecule [H = 1, O = 8] (c) Methane [C = 6, H = 1]
modelAnswer: (a) MgCl₂ (ionic). Mg (2,8,2) loses its 2 valence electrons, one to each of two Cl atoms (2,8,7). Diagram: Mg with two crosses (×) in its outer shell. Each × moves to a different Cl, which has 7 dots, giving [Mg]²⁺ and 2[:Cl:]⁻, each Cl⁻ with 8 electrons (7 dots + 1 cross). Mg²⁺ has the neon configuration (2,8) and each Cl⁻ the argon configuration (2,8,8). (b) H₂O (covalent). O (2,6) shares one electron pair with each of two H atoms. Diagram: H ×• O •× H, with two more lone pairs (4 dots) on O. O now has 8 electrons (2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs), each H has 2 (duplet), and there are 2 single covalent bonds. (c) CH₄ (covalent). C (2,4) shares one electron pair with each of four H atoms. Diagram: C at the centre with 4 shared pairs (•×) to H atoms above, below, left and right. C has an octet, each H a duplet, and there are 4 single covalent bonds with no lone pairs on C.
keyPoints: MgCl₂: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; each Cl gains 1e⁻ → Cl⁻ (ionic)
H₂O: 2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs on O (covalent)
CH₄: 4 shared pairs, octet on C, duplet on each H

text: Draw electron dot structures for the formation of: (a) Calcium oxide [Ca = 20, O = 8] (b) Carbon tetrachloride [C = 6, Cl = 17] (c) Oxygen molecule
modelAnswer: (a) CaO (ionic). Ca (2,8,8,2) transfers its 2 valence electrons to O (2,6), giving [Ca]²⁺ [:O:]²⁻. O²⁻ has 8 outer electrons (6 dots + 2 crosses), the neon configuration, and Ca²⁺ has the argon configuration (2,8,8). (b) CCl₄ (covalent). C (2,4) shares one electron pair with each of four Cl atoms (2,8,7). Each Cl keeps 3 lone pairs and gains a share of one pair, so it has an octet. C has an octet with 4 bond pairs. There are 4 single covalent bonds. (c) O₂ (covalent). Each O (2,6) needs 2 electrons, so the two O atoms share two pairs of electrons, a double bond (O=O). Each O keeps 2 lone pairs, so each has an octet (2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs).
keyPoints: CCl₄: 4 single covalent bonds, 3 lone pairs on each Cl
O₂: double covalent bond (O=O), 2 lone pairs on each O

text: (a) Draw the orbit structure for the formation of a nitrogen molecule. (b) What is meant by a 'lone pair of electrons'? Show the lone pairs in an orbit (electron dot) diagram of a water molecule.
modelAnswer: (a) Nitrogen (2,5) needs 3 more electrons. Two N atoms each contribute 3 electrons and share 3 pairs, forming a triple covalent bond, N≡N. Each N keeps 1 lone pair and has an octet (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair). (b) A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom only and is not shared in bond formation. In H₂O, oxygen (6 valence electrons) uses 2 electrons to form two O–H bond pairs (H ×• O •× H). Its remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, drawn as two pairs of dots on O. Water therefore has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs.
keyPoints: N₂: 3 shared pairs (triple bond), 1 lone pair on each N
Lone pair: valence electron pair not involved in bonding
H₂O: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs on oxygen

text: A compound has the formula H₂Y, where Y is a non-metal with 2 energy levels. State: (i) the electronic configuration of Y; (ii) the valency of Y; (iii) the type of bonding in H₂Y; (iv) the formula of the compound formed between calcium and Y.
modelAnswer: Y forms H₂Y, so it has valency 2. A non-metal with 2 shells and valency 2 is oxygen. (i) The configuration of Y is 2,6. (ii) The valency of Y is 2, since it needs 2 electrons to complete its octet. (iii) H₂Y (H₂O) has covalent bonding. Y shares one electron pair with each H atom. (iv) Calcium (valency 2) and Y (valency 2) combine 1:1, so the formula is CaY (CaO), an ionic compound.

text: Using only the ions Al³⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻, Ag⁺, OH⁻, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, S²⁻, CO₃²⁻, Hg²⁺, O²⁻ and Fe³⁺, give formulae for: (a) a nitrate P of a metal that decomposes on heating to give a solid residue and oxygen gas only; (b) a salt Q that decomposes in the presence of sunlight; (c) salt R formed when aluminium reacts with a greenish-yellow gas; (d) alkali S formed when sodium oxide is added to water; (e) salt T which on heating gives a metal used in thermometers, carbon dioxide and oxygen.
modelAnswer: (a) P = KNO₃. Nitrates of very reactive metals give the nitrite and oxygen only: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂. (b) Q = AgCl. It undergoes photochemical decomposition: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight). (c) R = AlCl₃. The greenish-yellow gas is chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. (d) S = NaOH: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH. (e) T = HgCO₃. Mercury is the thermometer metal: 2HgCO₃ → 2Hg + 2CO₂ + O₂.

text: Balance the following equations: (i) Cu(NO₃)₂ → CuO + NO₂ + O₂ (on heating) (ii) FeS₂ + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ (on heating) (iii) H₂S + O₂ → H₂O + SO₂ (iv) KMnO₄ + HCl → KCl + MnCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂
modelAnswer: (i) 2Cu(NO₃)₂ → 2CuO + 4NO₂ + O₂. (ii) 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂. (iii) 2H₂S + 3O₂ → 2H₂O + 2SO₂. (iv) 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂. Check for (iv): K 2 = 2; Mn 2 = 2; O 8 = 8; H 16 = 16; Cl 16 = 2 + 4 + 10.

text: Balance the following equations: (a) S + H₂SO₄ → SO₂ + H₂O (b) Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂ (c) P + HNO₃ → NO₂ + H₂O + H₃PO₄ (d) Pb₃O₄ + HCl → PbCl₂ + H₂O + Cl₂ (e) (NH₄)₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → NH₃ + H₂O + CaSO₄
modelAnswer: (a) S + 2H₂SO₄ → 3SO₂ + 2H₂O. (b) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (c) P + 5HNO₃ → 5NO₂ + H₂O + H₃PO₄. Check: H 5 = 2 + 3; N 5 = 5; O 15 = 10 + 1 + 4. (d) Pb₃O₄ + 8HCl → 3PbCl₂ + 4H₂O + Cl₂. (e) (NH₄)₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NH₃ + 2H₂O + CaSO₄.
